Our results suggest a generic, sound framework for ranking-function synthesis and, beyond termination, LLM-assisted synthesis of formally checkable liveness certificates, both of which represent new directions of software engineering research.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 24 pages, 6 pages

Logic in Computer Science.title: The Complexity of Data-Free Nfer
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Nfer is a Runtime Verification language for the analysis of event traces that applies rules to create hierarchies of time intervals. This work examines the complexity of the evaluation and satisfiability problems for the data-free fragment of nfer. The evaluation problem asks whether a given interval is generated by applying rules to a known input, while the satisfiability problem asks if an input exists that will generate a given interval.
  By excluding data from the language, we obtain polynomial-time algorithms for the evaluation problem and for satisfiability when only considering inclusive rules. Furthermore, we show decidability for the satisfiability problem for cycle-free specifications with a NExpTime lower bound and undecidability for satisfiability of full data-free nfer.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Machine-Checked Soundness of the GKR Protocol for Sparse-Merkle Updates
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Proofs of authenticated-data-structure updates built on the Goldwasser-Kalai-Rothblum (GKR) protocol are sound only if three arguments hold together: the soundness of the protocol, the exactness of the arithmetization that turns an update into a circuit, and the binding of the hash commitments. For GKR, the mechanizations we know of stop at the sumcheck subprotocol. For sparse-Merkle membership, non-membership and update as compiled by the StateSync-GKR prover, we machine-check in Isabelle/HOL the first two arguments, their composition, and the leaf side of the third. For layered circuits with linear, product and cube gates, the cube gate serving the $x^3$ S-box of Poseidon2, we prove that for a false output claim, the event that some layer's sumcheck accepts a false sum while all earlier carried claims are false has probability at most $(s_{\mathrm{out}} + \sum_i (2 s_i d_i + 1))/|\mathbb{F}|$, where layer $i$ has $2^{s_i}$ wires and $d_i$ bounds the degree of its sumcheck polynomial. We instantiate the bound over the exact quartic extension of the 31-bit KoalaBear field from which small-field provers draw challenges, so that the denominator is $p^4 \approx 2^{124}$, and lift base-field layers and false outputs into it. In a constraint-level model of the compiler, with the hash sub-circuits as abstract functions, the verifier model accepts exactly the valid transitions, and leaf-commitment collisions reduce to sponge collisions. Their composition is mechanized for claims that no witness makes valid, and from the mechanized theorems it follows on paper that the bad event has probability at most this bound for every input that does not encode a valid transition. All bounds concern the interactive public-coin protocol with uniform challenges; the Fiat-Shamir transformation, knowledge soundness and zero knowledge are outside the model.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 26 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables, 2 listings. v2 reorganizes the paper around its cryptographic statements, adds a per-input soundness corollary and a proof-engineering appendix, and corrects the description of the extension-field lifting; v1 theorem statements unchanged. Companion paper: arXiv:2610.14849. Software: https://github.com/Oraclizer/statesync-gkr (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23280552)

Logic in Computer Science.title: Quantitative Reachability Properties Beyond Decisiveness
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Decisiveness is central to reachability algorithms for infinite Markov chains, but is a qualitative notion: it guarantees that path-enumeration algorithms terminate, without an a priori bound on the horizon. We study decisiveness quantitatively of Markov chains, and apply our results to the approximate quantitative coverability problem for effective probabilistic well-structured transition systems (pWSTS). We introduce truncation sets, which represent the horizons sufficient to approximate the reachability probability within a precision $\varepsilon$. These sets reformulate decisiveness quantitatively, and their elements can be computed when it is decisive. To obtain such horizons, before any exploration, we introduce geometrically reachable sets, for which the probability of not reaching them within n steps decreases exponentially in n, up to a prefactor depending on the initial state. Horizons valid for all initial states exist iff this prefactor can be chosen uniformly for boundedly coarse chains. For such pWSTS, including probabilistic vector addition systems and Galton-Watson processes, we obtain a priori global horizons growing at most logarithmically in $1/\varepsilon$. In the non-uniform case, we give a drift condition ensuring the existence of a finite geometrically reachable set. Under this condition, we derive a priori horizons growing at most logarithmically in $1/\varepsilon$ and in the weight w(x) measuring the size of the initial state x. In both cases, we compute a horizon function whose evaluation on any initial state and precision requires only a constant number of elementary operations $(+, -, \times, / \text{ and } \log)$. For probabilistic lossy channel systems, this yields, to our knowledge, the first explicit a priori horizons from arbitrary initial states, and it extends to $ν$-pLCS, a new infinitely branching variant with probabilistic emissions.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 38 pages

Logic in Computer Science.title: A categorical formulation of Kraus' paradox
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We give a categorical formulation of Kraus' "magic trick" for recovering information from truncated types. Rather than type theory, we work in Van den Berg-Moerdijk path categories with a univalent universe, and rather than propositional truncation we work with arbitrary cofibrations, which includes truncation as a special case. We show, using Kraus' argument that any cofibration with homogeneous domain is a monomorphism. We give some simple concrete examples in groupoids to illustrate the interaction between homogeneous types, cofibrations and univalent fibrations.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Dynamic Planar Graph Isomorphism is in DynFO
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Consider two planar graphs which are subject to edge insertions and deletions. We show that whether the two graphs are isomorphic can be maintained with first-order logic formulas and auxiliary data of polynomial size. This places the dynamic planar graph isomorphism problem into the dynamic descriptive complexity class DynFO. As a consequence, there is a dynamic constant-time parallel algorithm with polynomial-size auxiliary data which maintains whether two dynamic planar graphs are isomorphic.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Full version of a LICS 2026 paper

Logic in Computer Science.title: Formal Explanations for Linear Temporal Logic over Finite Traces
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Linear Temporal Logic over Finite Traces (LTLf) is widely used in Artificial Intelligence to specify desired temporal behavior and determine whether finite traces satisfy or violate it. Explaining these outcomes is essential for debugging and trust. However, existing approaches typically capture either sufficient reasons or counterfactual causes, without clarifying their relationship. We introduce a native characterization of abductive (AXps) and contrastive (CXps) explanations directly over finite traces, based on locking and unlocking time-indexed events. We prove its equivalence to the classifier-based formulation, and show that CXps coincide with a recently proposed temporal causality semantics for LTLf. This characterization enables an efficient implementation based on the enumeration of minimal unsatisfiable cores and minimal correction sets of ASP programs. Experiments on real-world event logs demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.

Logic in Computer Science.title: SoK: Timestamps Are Not a Time Model: Rethinking Temporal Reasoning in Host-Based Intrusion Detection
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Host-based intrusion detectors order events, window audit streams and sequence attack stages by their timestamps. Every conclusion they draw therefore rests on assumptions about clocks, delivery, entity identity and the integrity of the evidence, and most of these assumptions go unstated. This Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) makes them explicit. Drawing on temporal databases, stream processing and runtime verification, we distill five components of a time model, together with a checklist of evidence assumptions and four levels of guarantee, and walk through a running campaign with them. A documented search yields fifteen families of detection and investigation. For papers selected by screening role and period, plus named systems and landmarks, we check the stated assumptions in the full texts, and we assess eleven temporal knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) formalisms and a learned baseline on nine attack patterns. Some early alert correlators stated clock and delivery assumptions, and forensics measures clock error. Current provenance-based detectors state no clock bound. Four audited papers describe input-ordering conditions or conventions, but none specifies conditions for conclusion validity across a stated class of delivery failures. In the selected provenance-based systems, campaign composition uses system-specific procedures or objectives, learned state, causal graph queries or language models, and beyond CEP-based query systems, we found no temporal rule language or stream reasoner from KRR applied to host audit data. In 28 of 38 audited provenance-era detector papers, capture or stored evidence is trusted or its manipulation is placed out of scope, and none says which conclusions survive deleted, delayed or forged records. Five open challenges follow from these gaps.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Extended version with full appendices (search method, KRR domain analysis, rating evidence, formalizations). 51 pages, 1 figure, 16 tables. Artifacts: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23530002

Logic in Computer Science.title: Unbelievably Complex
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We present the directed simplicial complex: this is an extension of a simplicial complex with a direction on its faces. This enables us to model a local notion of belief in a three-valued semantics, in which formulas may be true, false, or undefined. Of particular interest is a class of directed simplicial complexes called cups, in which any maximal set of vertices of different colors is a facet. Cups permit a more concise relational representation. We give examples and applications of our logical semantics. We then provide a sound and complete axiomatization for the class of directed simplicial complexes and extend it to an axiomatization for the class of cups. We include a detailed technical comparison with other works on belief on complexes. Our work generalizes a prior axiomatization for knowledge on (undirected) impure simplicial complexes.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Connecting Quantum Proof Systems and Hoare Logic
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Verifying quantum programs today requires specialized proof systems built on interactive theorem provers such as Rocq, Lean, Isabelle, or Why3, and even modest quantum algorithms cost substantial human effort to verify. Because quantum programs cannot be effectively checked by runtime testing, formal verification is the only viable path to correctness, making the cost of these bespoke systems the chief barrier to scalable quantum software assurance. We show that verifying a quantum program should be no harder than verifying a classical array program, a paradigm commonly used in parallel programming: the Qafny quantum proof system translates into Hoare logic with array theory completely (every Qafny proof becomes a valid Hoare triple) and soundly (a valid translated triple certifies only true quantum specifications), and we mechanize the completeness direction in Rocq. The embedding determinizes quantum proof obligations and exposes the full machinery of classical automated verifiers (e.g. Dafny and SMT-based separation logic) to quantum code, removing the need for dedicated quantum proof system infrastructure. In particular, the embedding supplies the correctness argument that the existing compilation of Qafny into Dafny lacks.

Signal Processing.title: AmbientFM: A Foundation Model for Ambient Sensing
Signal Processing.summary:
Ambient intelligence seeks to continuously understand human presence, activity, and physiology in physical spaces, enabling smart environments, health monitoring, and human-computer interaction. WiFi infrastructure offers a ubiquitous, always-on, and privacy-preserving sensing substrate across billions of IoT devices. Yet ambient sensing with WiFi remains largely fragmented, with most systems relying on task-specific models, labeled data collection, and customized training pipelines.
  We present AmbientFM, a foundation model for ambient sensing through ubiquitous WiFi signals. AmbientFM is pre-trained on 9.2 million unlabeled Channel State Information (CSI) samples collected over 439 days from 20 commercial device types deployed in real homes, the largest real-world WiFi CSI pre-training corpus reported to date. It learns transferable wireless representations through contrastive learning, masked reconstruction, and physics-informed objectives tailored to wireless signals. With lightweight adaptation, a single backbone transfers to 9 downstream tasks, achieving above 0.90 AUROC on all classification benchmarks and supporting dense spatial reconstruction. AmbientFM reduces the need for labeled data and task-specific design, enabling scalable ambient intelligence on existing wireless infrastructure.
Signal Processing.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Signal Processing.title: Frequency-Dependent Hybrid Digital and Microwave Linear Analog Computer (MiLAC) Beamforming for Multiuser MIMO-OFDM Systems
Signal Processing.summary: Microwave linear analog computing (MiLAC) has recently emerged as a promising approach for reducing the hardware and digital-processing requirements of large-scale multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems. In narrowband multiuser systems, hybrid digital-MiLAC beamforming can achieve digital beamforming flexibility with only as many radio-frequency (RF) chains as data streams. However, extending this advantage to wideband systems is nontrivial because practical MiLAC circuits exhibit frequency-dependent responses. In this paper, we investigate hybrid digital-MiLAC beamforming for multiuser MISO-OFDM systems with a frequency-dependent MiLAC circuit model. We characterize the frequency dependence of MiLAC by relating the susceptance of each tunable component across subcarriers to its center-frequency value. Under this frequency coupling, we show that a single MiLAC circuit generally cannot simultaneously match the desired beamforming directions across all subcarriers, highlighting the essential role of subcarrier-dependent digital precoding. We then develop a block coordinate descent (BCD) algorithm to jointly optimize the digital and MiLAC beamformers for average sum-rate maximization. In particular, an efficient alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm is custom-designed to handle the frequency-coupled circuit constraints in the MiLAC beamformer subproblem. Simulation results show that the proposed hybrid digital-MiLAC design outperforms conventional hybrid digital-analog beamforming, particularly when fewer RF chains are available and the channel is more frequency-selective. With $64$ transmit antennas and $4$ data streams, it attains $96.3\%$ of the digital sum-rate using only $8$ RF chains. Furthermore, under highly frequency-selective channels and using $4$ RF chains, it provides a $48\%$ sum-rate gain over the conventional hybrid design.

Signal Processing.title: Multi-view Semantic-aware Resource Allocation for Edge AI
Signal Processing.summary: Semantic communication is emerging as a pivotal paradigm to overcome wireless resource scarcity in 6G networks. This paper proposes a novel end-to-end framework for semantics-aware resource allocation in multi-user Edge AI. We extend the Opportunistic Information Bottleneck (OIB) to a multi-view setting, termed the Multi-view Gaussian Information Bottleneck (MGIB), by fusing complementary source views without variational approximation or network retraining. A resource allocation framework is then formulated for joint compression-level selection, transmission mode selection (i.e., the number of active sources per group), and PRB assignment. The problem is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP), solved efficiently via a proposed Lagrangian Relaxation (LR) algorithm, and benchmarked against the NP-hard optimal solution. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed LR scheme achieves near-optimal utility, and doubles PRB efficiency versus average allocation.
Signal Processing.comment: Submitted to IEEE Wireless Communications Letters. Jiawei Luo and Hussein Saleh contributed equally to this work

Signal Processing.title: Space-Time Stacked Intelligent Metasurfaces for Doppler-Resilient LEO Broadcasting
Signal Processing.summary: Stacked intelligent metasurfaces (SIMs) cascade programmable layers in front of a feed. In the SIM designs reported so far, including those proposed for low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites, the layer coefficients are space-only controls or are varied randomly in time to support opportunistic scheduling, so that every radiated beam carries the frequency of the feed. This paper introduces space-time SIMs (ST-SIMs), whose layers are modulated in time and use the temporal dimension of the stack deterministically: each spatial mode of the aperture is paired with its own prescribed frequency translation. The application is LEO broadcasting, where a common waveform reaches terminals with different Doppler shifts, and any common Doppler correction leaves residuals of up to half the Doppler span. We derive the harmonic-domain model of the stack, solve the minimum-energy space-frequency synthesis in closed form, and prove that full column rank of the steering matrix is necessary and sufficient for decoupling K terminal-specific translations, a result that extends to groups of terminals. We further propose a phase-only synthesis algorithm with guaranteed stationarity, together with quantization and control-rate laws. Simulations at 20 GHz over 50 random drops show that a four-layer ST-SIM with a single radio-frequency chain removes the Doppler floor of a static SIM for footprint radii above about 45 km and, under the ideal phase-only model and at equal radiated peak energy, approaches ideal digital per-terminal precompensation within 0.5 dB for resolvable terminals, whereas, in the evaluated geometries, a single time-modulated layer cannot synthesize the required modes.

Signal Processing.title: GNSS Anomaly Detection in Urban Canyons: A Comprehensive Survey of Multimodal Visibility Inference
Signal Processing.summary: Reliable GNSS positioning in dense urban environments depends on assessing satellite visibility and identifying measurements degraded by non-line-of-sight (NLOS) reception and multipath. This survey organizes reception-state inference into three complementary evidence families: receiver-side signals, 3D maps and environmental models, and auxiliary sensors. Receiver-side approaches span antenna/electromagnetic, tracking/baseband, and observable-domain evidence, interpreted through rule-based, statistical, machine-learning, and deep-learning methods. Map-based approaches are examined by reviewing environmental representations and methods such as geometric screening, shadow matching, 3D ray tracing, and neural implicit visibility prediction. IMU, camera, and LiDAR measurements provide complementary kinematic, visual, and geometric evidence for online screening. Across these families, we compare accuracy, interpretability, hardware and calibration requirements, map dependence, computational cost, and suitability for real-time deployment. We identify open challenges in dataset quality and labeling, domain generalization, map freshness, and resource-efficient implementation. The resulting synthesis connects signal processing, environmental modeling, and sensor fusion to guide the design of robust urban GNSS measurement-screening systems.
Signal Processing.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Aerospace and Electronic Systems Magazine. DOI: 10.1109/MAES.2026.3746915

Signal Processing.title: End-to-End Neural Modeling of EM Response and Design Performance for Free-Form RFIC Passives
Signal Processing.summary: Passive matching networks are critical components in radio-frequency integrated circuits (RFICs), but their design is bottlenecked by expensive finite-difference-based electromagnetic (EM) simulation. We propose an end-to-end neural framework for free-form RFIC passives that predicts both EM response and downstream design performance under varying frequency and circuit contexts, combining a frequency-conditioned neural simulator with a circuit-conditioned neural solver. To improve design performance prediction, the simulator outputs a neural EM response consisting of both the explicit EM response and a complementary response, together with a dependence regularizer that encourages the two responses to capture orthogonal information. To evaluate the proposed framework, we construct a large-scale dataset of free-form passive layouts, synthesized from both expert-designed contours and random paths. Our 21M-parameter model achieves high accuracy across a broad frequency range, circuit contexts and passive matching settings, with $R^2>0.98$ for almost all targets, while providing orders-of-magnitude faster evaluation than traditional EM simulation. Code available at https://github.com/ETH-IDEAS/RFIC-NeuralSim.
Signal Processing.comment: NeurIPS'26

Signal Processing.title: Synergizing Wireless Foundation Models and LLMs: A Multi-Task Framework for MA Systems
Signal Processing.summary: While movable antennas (MAs) provide enhanced spatial flexibility through dynamic repositioning, they confront critical challenges in acquiring complete channel state information (CSI) and efficiently optimizing antenna positions. Encouragingly, wireless foundation models (WFMs) capture generalizable channel priors for high-quality CSI extrapolation, while large language models (LLMs) enable parameter-efficient, token-level optimization for wireless tasks. In this paper, we synergistically integrate a WFM and an LLM into a multi-task framework for MA systems. First, to address the mismatch between existing WFM pre-training and MA channel characteristics, we develop an MA-oriented ``ExtLWM'' based on the large wireless model (LWM) architecture. Second, we design a unified ExtLWM-Connector-LLM architecture that flexibly adapts to different MA configurations without structural redesign. Third, we reformulate discrete MA positioning as a sequential decision-making problem, where candidate positions are represented by numerical tokens and optimized using group relative policy optimization (GRPO) to exploit the serial generation capability of the LLM. Finally, a multi-stage training strategy is developed to maintain multi-task performance under limited training samples while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Simulation results show that ExtLWM can produce high-quality channel embeddings while outperforming various benchmarks in CSI extrapolation. Meanwhile, the proposed LLM-based approach achieves a favorable trade-off between performance and computational complexity.
Signal Processing.comment: Accepted by IEEE JSTSP

Signal Processing.title: RIS-Assisted Downlink Pinching-Antenna Systems With NLOS Environments
Signal Processing.summary: This paper investigates a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted downlink pinching-antenna system (PASS) in the presence of non-line-of-sight (NLOS) users caused by unavoidable obstacles. An RIS is deployed to extend the coverage of the physically constrained PASS by establishing virtual line-of-sight (LOS) links. To improve system performance, we propose a zero-forcing (ZF) beamforming-based alternating optimization (AO) framework that minimizes the transmit power by jointly optimizing the RIS reflection coefficients and pinching-antenna (PA) activation positions. Specifically, the RIS reflection coefficients are optimized using the Riemannian conjugate gradient (RCG) method, while a novel projected gradient-based method is developed to efficiently optimize the PA activation positions. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed AO framework outperforms baseline schemes in terms of both transmit power and computational efficiency under different system configurations including the rate requirements and RIS sizes.
Signal Processing.comment: 6 pages, 4 figures

Signal Processing.title: Forecasting Ionospheric Irregularities on GNSS Lines of Sight Using Dynamic Graphs with Ephemeris Conditioning
Signal Processing.summary: Most data-driven ionospheric models operate on gridded products, which do not preserve the time-varying sampling structure of satellite-based sensing. We instead model the ionosphere as a dynamic graph over ionospheric pierce points, with connectivity that evolves as satellite positions change. Because satellite trajectories are predictable, the graph topology over the forecast horizon can be constructed in advance. We exploit this property to condition forecasts on the future graph structure, which we term ephemeris conditioning. This enables prediction on lines of sight (LoS) that appear only in the forecast horizon. We evaluate our framework on Global Navigation Satellite System data from a co-located receiver pair in Singapore spanning 2023 to 2025. The task is forecasting irregularities defined by the Rate of TEC Index (ROTI) up to 2 hours ahead as per-node binary classification. The resulting model, IonoDGNN, achieves a Brier Skill Score (BSS) of 0.55 and an area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC) of 0.77. These correspond to improvements over persistence of 53% in BSS and 58% in PR-AUC, with larger gains at longer lead times. Ablations confirm that graph structure and ephemeris conditioning each contribute meaningfully. Under simulated coverage dropout, the model retains predictive skill on affected nodes through spatial message passing from observed neighbors. Compared to interpolation baselines, the proposed model achieves better recovery, especially at higher dropout levels. These results suggest that dynamic graph forecasting on evolving LoS is a viable alternative for ionospheric modeling. The project and the dataset are available at https://github.com/Mert-chan/IonoDGNN.
Signal Processing.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing. 13 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables

Signal Processing.title: Fading Suppression in Distributed Acoustic Sensing Using Frequency-Domain Replica Reconstruction and Noise-Whitened Principal Component Combining
Signal Processing.summary: Frequency-selective Rayleigh fading in distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) based on phase-sensitive optical time-domain reflectometry (phi-OTDR) calls for effective diversity, but existing rotated-vector-sum (RVS) combining of nonoverlapping subbands incurs a spatial-resolution penalty. In this letter, we propose frequency-domain replica reconstruction and noise-whitened principal component combining (PCC) that combines a full-band replica and overlapping subbands using fixed weights estimated across probing periods after whitening correlated replica noise. This approach retains wider subbands and reduces reliance on noisy first-period alignment, balancing diversity with nominal spatial resolution. Experiments over approximately 7.1 km of fiber with 16-microsecond linear frequency-modulated (LFM) pulses recover 500-Hz vibrations with reduced background phase excursions and a 2.46-2.76-dB improvement in the vibration-to-background ratio (VBR) over the first-period RVS.
Signal Processing.comment: This work has been submitted for potential publication

Signal Processing.title: Environment-Adaptive Dynamic KV Cache for Multi-Path Parameter Prediction
Signal Processing.summary: Multipath parameter prediction provides a structured and physically interpretable representation of wireless propagation for environment-aware communication systems. However, existing Transformer-based methods repeatedly encode the same environment when predicting multiple BS--UE links, resulting in redundant computation. To address this issue, we propose an environment-conditioned dynamic KV caching framework for multipath parameter prediction. Specifically, we decouple environment-dependent computation from BS--UE geometry, enabling environment-side representations and intermediate KV states to be reused across multiple link queries while only the geometry branch is updated. Building on this reusable cache, we further introduce a dynamic compression mechanism that uses environment-side attention scores to retain informative tokens and adaptively allocates a fixed cache budget across Transformer layers. Experiments on the WAIR-D dataset show that the proposed method reduces KV memory from 0.2500 MB to 0.1406 MB, while the delay NMSE increases only slightly from 0.0673 to 0.0678. Code is available at https://github.com/LZhaoyang/kv.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Inductive Grounded Arithmetic: Goodstein, the Hydra, and $Γ_0$
Logic in Computer Science.summary: What does a recursive definition mean when the logic is grounded, so a sentence is true only if a terminating process makes it so? Kripke's answer for the special case of truth was the least fixed point. This paper takes that answer as a rule. Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) already writes any recursive definition as one self-referential term, paradoxes included. Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA) adds the elimination rule for every positive one, so that accessibility, the winning positions of a game, and grounded truth itself each come with their own induction principle. The rule is sound for the omega model and the system is consistent, both machine-checked in Isabelle/HOL. With the rule, IGA proves Goodstein's theorem outright, in a logic without implication at an undecided hypothesis, and the Kirby-Paris hydra game for primitive recursive strategies, both with every step of the arithmetic a grounded derivation. It proves the Cantor normal forms well-founded, from which the well-foundedness of the standard $\varepsilon_0$ notation system in HOL follows, and it certifies the Veblen notation as an ordinal below every $\varphi(n,0)$. It defines Kripke truth for RGA's own language as one fixed point that agrees with the omega model exactly. Two equivalences locate what the classical world has and the grounded one does not. IGA proves the whole Veblen notation well-founded exactly when it admits bivalence of accessibility for that order, and bivalence of accessibility for an order is sound exactly when the order is well-founded; so $Γ_0$ lies at most one instance of excluded middle away, at the accessibility predicate of the notation, and that instance, the well-foundedness sentence and one membership claim in a primitive-recursive form of Kleene's $\mathcal O$ are interderivable over IGA.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Propositional formula minimization is $Σ_2^p$-complete under many-one reductions
Logic in Computer Science.summary: The Minimum Equivalent Expression problem (MEE) asks, given a propositional formula $φ$ and an integer $k$, whether $φ$ is equivalent to a formula with at most $k$ occurrences of propositional variables. While the problem is clearly in $Σ_2^p$, its completeness under polynomial-time many-one reductions has remained open since at least 1979. Buchfuhrer and Umans showed in 2008 that it is $Σ_2^p$-complete under polynomial-time Turing reductions. In this note, we present a proof discovered by GPT-Sol-6.1 which establishes that MEE is $Σ_2^p$-complete also under polynomial-time many-one reductions.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Proceedings Twelfth International Conference on Non-Classical Logics. Theory and Applications
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Non-Classical Logics. Theory and Applications (NCL) is an international conference aimed at presenting novel results and survey papers in the broad field of non-classical logics and their applications. The first two editions were held in Ł{ó}d{ź}, Poland, in September 2008 and 2009. Subsequent editions were organised in Toru{ń} (2010, 2012, 2015, 2018) and Ł{ó}d{ź} (2011, 2013, 2016, 2022, 2024). The tenth edition of the conference, organised by the University of Ł{ó}d{ź} in 2022, was the first to have its proceedings published in EPTCS. We are honoured and pleased to continue this practice and, for the third time, include all accepted long papers in an EPTCS volume. Furthermore, for the first time, we have also included all accepted extended abstracts in the volume.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Partial Rewriting and Value Interpretation of Logically Constrained Terms (Full Version)
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Logically constrained term rewrite systems (LCTRSs) are a rewriting formalism that naturally supports built-in data structures, including integers and bit-vectors. The recent framework of existentially constrained terms and most general constrained rewriting on them (Takahata et al., 2025) has many advantages over the original approach of rewriting constrained terms. In this paper, we introduce partial constrained rewriting, a variant of rewriting existentially constrained terms whose underlying idea has already appeared implicitly in previous analyses and applications of LCTRSs. We examine the differences between these two notions of constrained rewriting. First, we establish a direct correspondence between them, leveraging subsumption and equivalence of constrained terms where appropriate. Then we give characterizations of each of them, using the interpretation of existentially constrained terms by instantiation. We further introduce the novel notion of value interpretation, that highlights subtle differences between partial and most general rewriting.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Case Studies in Generalized Kantorovich-Rubinstein Duality
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
The classical Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality guarantees coincidence between metrics on the space of probability distributions defined on the one hand via transport plans (couplings) and on the other hand via price functions. Both constructions have been lifted to the level of generality of set functors, with the construction based on couplings referred to as the Wasserstein or simply the coupling-based lifting, and the price-function-based construction as the Kantorovich or codensity lifting, both based on a choice of quantitative modalities for the given functor. It is known that every coupling-based lifting can be expressed as a price-function-based lifting; however, the latter in general needs to use additional modalities. We give an example showing that this cannot be avoided in general. We refer to cases in which the same modalities can be used as satisfying the generalized Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. We establish the generalized Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality in this sense for two important cases: The Lévy-Prokhorov distance on distributions, which finds wide-spread applications in machine learning due to its favourable stability properties, and the standard metric on convex sets of distributions that arises by combining the Hausdorff and Kantorovich-Rubinstein distances.
  Furthermore we generalize (coupling-based) functor liftings from set functors to functors which act on (pseudo-)metric spaces, thus incorporating new example functors that map to closed subsets respectively Radon measures.

Logic in Computer Science.title: EntailLLM: Verifying Agent-Generated Vulnerability Discovery Paths with Domain Knowledge via Logic Programming
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Large language model agents are increasingly used to analyze potential software vulnerabilities, but their outputs can silently violate domain knowledge, limiting their reliability in safety-critical settings such as medical devices. Prior work either treats that output as a prediction to be scored or constrains it to walks within a single knowledge graph; neither checks whether reasoning over a binary is entailed by an independent body of domain knowledge. We present EntailLLM, a framework that includes a specialized LLM agent and a validation mechanism. The agent proposes a traversal path of the function call graph for a vulnerability, which is checked against a separate knowledge graph and a logic program by an entailment procedure under annotated logic. We evaluate EntailLLM by examining six specialized agents across three CWE classes, and eight binaries varying in size from 405 to 12,696 functions. The agents improve pooled entailment from 77% to 98%, with entailment decreasing in only 3 of 118 configurations. We found that the best-performing agent combines self-refinement and a priori domain knowledge. EntailLLM is deployed end-to-end on real medical-device binaries, reaching 98% pooled entailment without per-device tuning. Our framework inherits the formal guarantees of generalized annotated logic, providing logical verification of agent output that is both explainable and grounded in well-defined semantics.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Vector space embeddings of modal logic formulas: theory and application
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Reasoning tasks over modal logics are notoriously difficult, comprising problems which are often semi-decidable. Hence, it is not rare for applications leveraging such tasks to exploit heuristic approaches able to give results in an acceptable amount of time, at the cost of some inaccuracies. Some approaches may benefit from vector embeddings, allowing for instance to involve neural networks and machine learning models in the reasoning process. This work aims at providing a new way to provide such embeddings specifically for the modal case, aiming for faster reasoning through both mathematical and learning techniques.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Presented at the ESSLLI 2025 Student Session, Bochum. An extended version appeared as "Semantic Embeddings for Modal Logic (Extended Abstract)", ICTCS 2026, CEUR-WS Vol-4269, pp. 30-35. Code: https://github.com/aclai-lab/ESSLLI2025

Logic in Computer Science.title: Internal Reasoning and Consistency in Reflective Grounded Arithmetic
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) is a paracomplete arithmetic allowing direct expression of any general-recursive computation. Every RGA term is a program and truth is grounded evaluation, with a proof certificate at each universal quantifier. This paper shows, in a machine-checked Isabelle/HOL development, that such a system is powerful enough to carry out its own metamathematics. A fuel-indexed decider of RGA's grounded semantics and checkers for RGA's proofs are compiled primitive-recursive RGA terms. RGA proves internally that its decider never affirms $0 = 1$, and that every well-formed term it affirms has an RGA proof accepted by a transparent test. RGA proves that, for each valid RGA proof, its conclusion is true. RGA proves that each grounded-true well-formed term is provable. RGA proves that no proof in either of two decided classes of RGA proofs derives $0 = 1$.
  Gödel's incompleteness theorems hold for RGA, but their proofs must be adapted. In RGA an implication $A \rightarrow B$ is strictly stronger than an entailment $A \vdash B$: RGA discharges a hypothesis only when it can prove the hypothesis decided, a restriction needed to defuse Curry's paradox. RGA's implication is material and RGA has the disjunction property, so RGA proves no implication between ungrounded sentences. The implications that the textbook proof of Gödel's second theorem uses are of this kind and fail, but the entailments and rules it uses hold: Gödel's proof survives as entailments. RGA does not prove its consistency sentence $\mathit{Con}$: RGA carries out Gödel's argument internally, with a decided proof predicate and explicit proof transformers, and only the last step, that RGA does not prove $0 = 1$, is left to HOL. RGA also proves its own second incompleteness theorem as an entailment from $\mathit{Con}$, and as a single sentence quantified over proofs.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: title adjusted and substantially revised; now 177 pages

Logic in Computer Science.title: A Lambda Calculus Based on Quantum Logic
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We propose a typed lambda calculus based on quantum logic. We first present a natural deduction system for quantum logic with the Sasaki hook as its implication operation and then formulate a typed lambda calculus connected to this system through the Curry-Howard correspondence. We prove soundness and completeness of the former with respect to orthomodular lattices and strong normalization of the latter. The resulting lambda calculus has the characteristic feature that only one assumption is available in the typing derivation that serves as the premise of $λ$-abstraction. Under this restriction, ordinary currying is not available in general, but it is still possible to perform $λ$-abstraction by combining multiple assumptions into a single argument of product type and to construct a term corresponding to a deduction using the Sasaki projection.

Logic in Computer Science.title: h1: A Taste of the Bitter Lesson in Automated Theorem Proving
Logic in Computer Science.summary: While progress in informal mathematics has come largely from scaling the chain-of-thought and agentic reasoning of frontier language models, formal theorem proving has increasingly relied on human-designed workflows around these models, such as planning, decomposition, and orchestrating specialized provers. This raises a bitter-lesson question: can a simple agentic loop that scales test-time compute match these workflows? The answer matters as formal verification must scale to keep up with frontier models producing research mathematics, yet new workflows rarely settle it, as their gains are often confounded with stronger models or more compute. We study this question with h1, a simple harness that gives a model an efficient interface to Lean 4 and keeps it working through verifier feedback and self-reflection, without imposing a decomposition or search structure. h1 reaches state-of-the-art results on PutnamBench, FATE-X, and FormalConjectures100-Solved, settles eight open problems in FormalConjectures, and, at matched models, matches or outperforms specialized workflows such as Goedel-Architect and AlphaProof Nexus, surprisingly showing that a single attempt (pass@1) can often scale to solve open problems. Through ablations and matched-model comparisons with Claude Code and AxProverBase, we find that simplicity alone is not enough: an efficient Lean interface largely determines cost and solve rate. We thus recommend that future work evaluate frontier models with efficient execution feedback before prescribing workflows, at the risk of bitter lessons.

Logic in Computer Science.title: A Degree--Size Relation for Resolution over Polynomials
Logic in Computer Science.summary:
For every constant-width CNF, we show that linear degree in polynomial calculus (PC) implies exponential size in resolution over constant-degree polynomials, over the same prime field.
  Applications include exponential lower bounds for CNFs in $\operatorname{Res}(\operatorname{PC}_r/\mathbb{F}_p)$ and hence in $\operatorname{Res}(\oplus_p)$, separations between different moduli, improved lower bounds for $\operatorname{Res}(k)$ up to $k=\varepsilon\log n$, proof-search consequences, and an implication of super-polynomial $AC^0[p]$-Frege bounds from very strong PC degree lower bounds.
  The proof uses the common-multiplier idea isolated from Braun [arXiv:2609.23015] to construct a Razborov--Smolensky approximation that preserves inferences, without introducing extension variables. The approximation errors are measured by ranks of the multiplication maps induced by the error-witness polynomials, modulo bounded-degree PC consequences.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: Parameters in Section 8 (Conclusions) made explicit

Logic in Computer Science.title: Meta-Mathematics of Algebraic Complexity
Logic in Computer Science.summary: We initiate the study of the meta-mathematics of algebraic circuit lower bounds, aiming both to gain insight into the methods sufficient and necessary to prove algebraic circuit lower bounds, and to contribute to the study of bounded arithmetic as a logical foundation for complexity lower bounds. We demonstrate that while algebraic circuit lower bounds are hard for somewhat weak proof systems such as Polynomial Calculus Resolution ($\mathsf{PCR}$), contemporary lower bounds are efficiently provable in proof systems and bounded arithmetic theories corresponding to $\mathsf{NC}^2$, such as $\mathsf{VNC}^2$ and the corresponding class of propositional Frege proofs of quasipolynomial-size. Moreover, going below $\mathsf{VNC}^2$ into algebraic constant-depth reasoning is likely insufficient to efficiently prove already constant-depth algebraic circuit lower bounds. Under an algebraic analogue of the Krajicek--Razborov conjecture, our results suggest that proving superpolynomial lower bounds for general algebraic circuits will require stronger reasoning than that used in the rank-based proofs studied here. Specifically, we show the following.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: A preliminary version of this work appeared in the proceedings of ACM-IEEE LICS 2026

Logic in Computer Science.title: Numina Fuse: Interactive Autoformalization in Lean 4
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Numina Fuse is an agent-native application for formalizing mathematics in Lean 4. Since Lean can compile while not representing its intended informal meaning, and agents now write Lean faster than people can read it, we built Fuse around human supervision of agent work. A user works with an AI orchestrator on a Lean project and supervises it through views of the blueprint, the dependency graph, and the Lean code, while the backend keeps the project's derived state and runs agents for hours without the user present. We describe the development of Fuse throughout 2026, as it moved from a prescribed pipeline of agents paced by human review to an orchestrator that dispatches specialists, provers, and parallel children on its own. We designed for this shift, keeping project state, tooling, and interface design separate from orchestration so that agents could take over more of the work as models improved. We report Fuse's use in a formalization of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and a study of prover models. We close with lessons for the next generation of autoformalization systems. Fuse Desktop, an open-source local version, is available at https://github.com/project-numina/fuse-desktop.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 16 pages, 10 figures

Logic in Computer Science.title: A note reviewing Turing's 1936
Logic in Computer Science.summary: By closely rereading the original Turing's 1936 article, we can gain insight about that it is based on the claim to have defined a number which is not computable, arguing that there can be no machine computing the diagonal on the enumeration of the computable sequences. This article provides a careful analysis of Turing's original argument, demonstrating that it cannot be regarded as a conclusive proof. Furthermore, it shows that there is no evidence supporting the existence of a defined number that is not computable.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 14 pages, for more information see http://paolacattabriga.wordpress.com/

Logic in Computer Science.title: A Model-Theoretic Formalization of AlKhwaremis ilm alfaraid
Logic in Computer Science.summary: This paper presents a model theoretic and computational formalization of AlKhwarizmis treatment of inheritance within the framework of Computational Fiqh. We first show that every inheritance configuration in a specified class is representable as a finite system of rational linear equalities and inequalities, and that such systems are decided exactly by Fourier Motzkin elimination over Q. We then define the fixed dimensional inheritance structure Vd with distinguished claimant coordinates, and prove that every admissible rational linear coordinate realization is isomorphic to Vd, this establishes the algebraic representation as canonical within that class. The complete first order theory Td of Vd is shown to be complete by construction and is explicitly distinguished from the decidability of the inheritance relevant fragment. The methodological principle is then related to a broader formalization of closed Fiqh domains via exhaustive case generation, Horn clause axiomatization, and terminating deduction, yielding domain relative computational completeness.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 27 pages, 1 figure

Logic in Computer Science.title: Two Uncertainties Are Not One: Disagreement versus Decision-Risk in Cheap Structured Content Moderation
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Content moderation compresses a graded, contested human judgment into a binary act (leave up / take down) over billions of items, at a scale where running a frontier LLM on every post is uneconomical. A new class of frozen "System One" models returns typed, calibrated decisions instead of text at ~USD 0.000025 per call and ~100 ms. We run the first independent audit of one such model on 142,658 human-labeled comments, and benchmark it against 14 frontier reasoning models (the GPT-5.x, Claude, Gemini 3, and Grok families) on a shared probe set. Two findings stand out. First, the cheap model is accuracy-competitive: its zero-shot classification AUROC (0.83) is not statistically separable (paired bootstrap, n=56; a failure to reject parity, not proof of equivalence) from 13 of the 14 frontier systems while costing 1-3 orders of magnitude less, and it is no worse calibrated than several of them. Second, "confidence" conflates two uncertainties that come apart: human disagreement (where annotators split on satire and coded language) and decision risk (where the automatic action is costly-wrong). Under an asymmetric moderation loss these call for opposite escalation signals, so no single confidence number serves both. Because the model prices extra questions at nearly zero, decomposing the judgment into parallel sub-questions and reading their spread recovers a human-disagreement signal that the model's native confidence misses -- but this remedy is specific: it helps the weakest, disagreement-blind models and only when the decomposition aligns with the sources of disagreement; a specialist toxicity model and the strongest LLMs do not need it, and the effect is distribution-sensitive. We will release the instrument, the cached runs, and the analysis.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables

Logic in Computer Science.title: Choosing What to Observe: Higher-Order Obstructions in Horn Abduction
Logic in Computer Science.summary: An explanation may exist in every complete context yet be impossible to select from the information observed. We study this distinction in finite propositional Horn abduction with integrity constraints. Observations are sufficient when each report admits one hypothesis set that is consistent and entails the manifestation in every compatible context. We characterize sufficiency by minimal context families with no common explanation. Their variable spans form a canonical hypergraph whose transversals are exactly the sufficient observation sets. The characterization recovers classical discernibility for unique explanations and supports composition across independent components. Minimal obstructions have unbounded cardinality even for acyclic rules, while rectangular explanation families admit a tight bound given by their largest choice domain. With circuit-defined contexts, sufficiency is $Π_3^P$-complete and selecting at most $k$ observable variables is $Σ_4^P$-complete, already for unrestricted contexts and acyclic rules. The selection reduction makes observation choices enforce globally fixed existential commitments. Explicit contexts reduce both tasks to NP-complete problems; tabulated explanation families make sufficiency polynomial. These results connect explanatory choice, information requirements, and representation cost.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 9 pages, 1 figure

Logic in Computer Science.title: Shapes from Examples: Foundations of Shape Learning in Recursive SHACL
Logic in Computer Science.summary: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. We investigate the well-known fitting approach to this task: given sets P and N of positive and negative example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C, possibly using shape names defined in a recursive shape catalogue, that validates at every node in P and none in N. We focus on the case where C is written in a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI*. For the catalogue, we consider the well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. We address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems, and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: full version of a paper accepted at ISWC26

Logic in Computer Science.title: Expressivity Results for Structured Argumentation Frameworks with Uncertain Rules and Premises
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Modelling qualitative uncertainty in formal argumentation is essential both for practical applications and theoretical understanding. Yet, most existing work focuses on abstract models of argumentation under uncertainty. Following a recent trend in the literature, we tackle the open question of studying plausible instantiations of these abstract models. To do so, we root the uncertainty of arguments in their components in structured models: rules and premises. Our main conceptual contribution is to provide an intuitive notion of comparative expressivity suitable for both abstract and structured formalisms. Roughly, one formalism for arguing with qualitative uncertainty is at least as expressive as another if the former can generate the same set of abstract argumentation frameworks (completions) as the latter. On the technical side, we prove negative and positive results comparing the expressivity of abstract and structured models of argumentation with uncertainty. These results concern incomplete abstract argumentation frameworks and their extension with dependencies on the abstract side, and ASPIC$^+$, assumption-based argumentation (ABA) and deductive argumentation on the structured side.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Non-Expansive Fuzzy Modal Logic Has Uniform Interpolation
Logic in Computer Science.summary: Fuzzy logics with truth values in the unit interval vary in their choice of propositional connectives and their semantics, ranging from just minimum and maximum as in Zadeh logics to truncated addition and subtraction as in Łukasiewicz logics or their extensions with truth constants, known as Pavelka logics. In the more specific world of fuzzy modal logics, non-expansive fuzzy modal logic has recently been proposed as a sweet spot between Łukasiewicz (more precisely, Pavelka) and Zadeh fuzzy modal logic; it restricts Łukasiewicz propositional connectives to have one argument constant, equivalently extends the Zadeh propositional base with constant shift operators. It retains reasonable expressiveness both in practical terms and abstractly; in particular, it characterizes the standard notion of behavioural distance on fuzzy Kripke frames. At the same time, it allows for satisfiability checking in the same complexity as for its two-valued correspondent (the modal logic K, or the description logic ALC), in contrast to the notorious computational hardness of Łukasiewicz modal logic. In the present work, we show that non-expansive fuzzy modal logic admits uniform interpolation, a key property in modularization, information hiding, summarization, and other applications that fails for both Łukasiewicz (or Pavelka) and Zadeh modal logic.

Logic in Computer Science.title: Adversarial Problems and the Limits of Uniform Resolution
Logic in Computer Science.summary: A general method of resolution can take part in forming problems once their language represents the method itself. A fixed formation rule gives each sound resolver a presentation it cannot answer. Admitting the diagnosis yields a sound successor with an instance of its own. For standard arithmetical theories $\mathrm{T}$, the instance is $\mathsf{HA}$-provably equivalent to $\mathrm{Con}(\mathrm{T})$. A theory that decides its own instance asserts a false sentence. The $m$-th iterated independence question is equivalent to the instance $m$ stages later. No effective admission policy with consistent union closes the regress. A noncomputable answer function resolves all program indices, while a false assertion of resolution supplies no warrant. At feasible scale, bounded self-consistency is cheap. A clocked Gödel sentence gives an unconditional gap relative to its short binary description, but no superpolynomial lower bound in the window size. The arithmetic identity motivates studying bounded consistency of the successor theory, as in a conjecture of Pudlák. We state its finitely axiomatized case and prove that it implies $\mathcal{NP}\ne\mathrm{co}\mathcal{NP}$. The conjecture motivates a feasible analogue, but does not establish all clauses of the unbounded barrier.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 24 pages, 2 figures, Major revision with new title. The obstruction is now proved without reflection through a fixed formation rule on resolvers, the identity of the trap with Con(T), and a tower of iterated independence; the feasible regime is treated only conditionally, and no complexity separation is claimed

Logic in Computer Science.title: DeFAb: A Dataset for Grounded Scientific Discovery through Defeasible Abduction
Logic in Computer Science.summary: A theory can accommodate a counterexample by adding an exception. The harder problem is deciding how far the exception should extend and which predictions should survive. We present DeFAb, a dataset and symbolic verification framework built from curated biological knowledge in the Gene Ontology. Models fill gaps in a theory or propose exceptions to its rules. A verifier checks the consequences of each edit, allowing different solutions to receive credit. Simple symbolic repairs solve all 336 tasks in the released evaluation panel. This result exposes a limitation of the revision test. An exception tied to one entity can succeed without identifying a pattern that applies to other cases. We develop a contextual task that requires an exception to reach the relevant cases and preserve predictions elsewhere. Two planned studies compare training with verified and rejected examples, and revision with and without feedback about consequences. DeFAb makes the scope of a proposed explanation testable, providing a controlled step toward studying theory revision in scientific reasoning.
Logic in Computer Science.comment: 12 pages, 3 figures
